When I signed up to be a Seagoing Cowboy, I had no idea how much my life would change. I was just a young man looking for adventure, but what I found was something far greater—a chance to see the world, help people in need, and grow into a more capable, confident version of myself. If you are looking for an experience that will challenge you and reward you in equal measure, I encourage you to join the Seagoing Cowboys program.

Beyond the adventure, the work itself gave me a deep sense of purpose. Caring for the animals during the voyage was not always easy—it required patience, hard work, and responsibility, especially when the seas grew rough and the animals grew anxious. But knowing that these animals would help struggling farmers rebuild their livelihoods after the destruction of war made every difficult task worthwhile. I was not just a passenger on these ships; I was part of something bigger than myself, contributing to the recovery of entire communities.

Finally, the program shaped who I am as a person. I learned skills I never expected to learn, from handling livestock to working alongside a crew of people from different backgrounds. I gained confidence in my ability to adapt to new situations, whether that meant navigating a ship in a storm or communicating with people in a foreign country. These lessons have stayed with me long after my voyages ended.

In conclusion, the Seagoing Cowboys program offers adventure, purpose, and personal growth all in one experience. I saw the world, helped rebuild communities in need, and became a stronger, more capable person along the way. If you want a life-changing journey that combines hard work with meaningful impact, I urge you to consider joining the Seagoing Cowboys program yourself.

Prompt: Your principal is reconsidering the school's cell phone policy. She is considering two possible policies: 
Policy 1: Allow students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch periods and other free times, as long as the phones are turned off during class time. 
Policy 2: Do not allow students to have phones at school at all.
Write a letter to your principal convincing her which policy you believe is better. Support your position with specific reasons.
full_text:
Dear Principal Reyes,

I am writing to share my perspective on the cell phone policy currently under review. After considering both options, I believe Policy 1—allowing students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch and free periods, provided they remain off during class—is the more practical and beneficial choice for our school community.

First, this policy respects the reality of students' lives outside the classroom. Many students rely on their phones to coordinate rides home, check in with working parents, or manage schedules for after-school jobs and activities. A complete ban would create unnecessary stress and logistical headaches for families who depend on this communication. Policy 1 acknowledges these needs while still maintaining clear boundaries during instructional time.

Second, teaching responsible technology use is arguably more valuable than removing the temptation altogether. If students never have the opportunity to practice self-regulation with their phones, they miss a chance to develop skills they will need in college and the workplace, where phones are rarely banned outright but instead used with discretion. By allowing phones during designated free times, we give students a low-stakes environment to learn when it is appropriate to use technology and when it is not. This mirrors real-world expectations far better than a total prohibition.

Third, a full ban is likely to be difficult to enforce and could create more problems than it solves. Students determined to have their phones will find ways to hide them, leading to a cat-and-mouse dynamic between students and staff that wastes time and erodes trust. Policy 1, by contrast, reduces the incentive to sneak phones into class since students know they will have designated times to use them.

Finally, allowing phone use during lunch and free periods does not mean chaos will ensue. Many schools have successfully implemented similar policies, using clear consequences for violations, such as confiscation for a first offense during class time, to reinforce expectations. This balanced approach shows trust in students while still holding them accountable.

I understand the concerns that motivate considering a full ban, particularly around distraction and cyberbullying. However, these issues are best addressed through clear rules, consistent enforcement, and ongoing conversations about digital citizenship rather than an outright ban that treats all students as incapable of responsibility.

I hope you will consider Policy 1 as the more balanced and forward-thinking option. It respects student autonomy, prepares them for real-world expectations, and remains enforceable in practice.

Thank you for considering student input on this important decision.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student

Dear Principal Martinez,

I am writing to share my thoughts on the question of whether all students should be required to perform community service. After considering both sides of this issue, I believe that requiring community service would benefit our school and community, and I hope you will consider implementing this policy.

I understand that some students feel community service takes away valuable time from homework, sports, jobs, or family responsibilities. This concern is reasonable, and I think any requirement should be flexible enough to accommodate different schedules. However, the benefits of community service far outweigh this drawback.

First, community service teaches skills that classroom learning cannot always provide. My friend Maria tutors elementary school children twice a week, and she has told me that explaining math problems to younger students has actually improved her own understanding of the subject. She has also become more patient and learned how to communicate complicated ideas simply. These are skills that will help her in college and in her future career, regardless of what she chooses to study.

Second, service projects help students feel connected to their community. My friend Jake spends his Saturday mornings picking up litter along the river near our school. He told me that before he started this project, he rarely thought about the environment around him. Now he notices litter everywhere and feels a sense of responsibility to keep public spaces clean. This kind of awareness benefits everyone, not just Jake.

Third, community service can expose students to career paths and social issues they might not otherwise encounter. A required service program could introduce students to hospitals, animal shelters, food banks, or environmental organizations. Some students might discover a passion for nursing, social work, or environmental science simply because a service requirement gave them the opportunity to try something new.

Finally, requiring service sends an important message: that our school values contribution to the community, not just individual achievement. Grades and test scores matter, but so does learning to think beyond ourselves. If students are required to complete even ten or fifteen hours per year, they will graduate with firsthand experience of what it means to help others.

I recognize that implementation should be thoughtful. Perhaps students could choose from a variety of approved projects, or complete service over the summer to avoid conflicts with the school year schedule. This flexibility would address the concerns of students who feel too busy while still ensuring that everyone participates.

Thank you for considering this request. I believe a community service requirement would make our school stronger and would help every student grow, both academically and personally.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student

Prompt: Some of your friends perform community service. For example, some tutor elementary school children and others clean up litter. They think helping the community is very important. But other friends of yours think community service takes too much time away from what they need or want to do. 
Your principal is deciding whether to require all students to perform community service. 
Write a letter to your principal in which you take a position on whether students should be required to perform community service. Support your position with examples.
full_text:
Dear Principal Martinez,

I am writing to share my thoughts on the proposal to require all students to perform community service. After considering the arguments on both sides, I believe that requiring community service would benefit our school and community, and I hope you will consider implementing this policy.

I understand that some of my classmates worry that community service will take valuable time away from homework, sports, jobs, or family responsibilities. This is a legitimate concern, and I don't dismiss it lightly. Students already juggle demanding schedules, and adding another obligation can feel overwhelming. However, I believe the benefits of required service outweigh these drawbacks, especially if the program is thoughtfully designed.

First, community service teaches skills that classroom learning cannot fully provide. My friend Sarah tutors elementary school children twice a week, and she has told me that explaining math problems to third graders has actually improved her own understanding of the material while teaching her patience and communication skills. These are qualities that will help her in college and future careers, regardless of her chosen field.

Second, service connects students to their community in meaningful ways. My friend Marcus, who picks up litter in our local park, has mentioned that he now feels a sense of ownership over that space. He notices when others litter and picks it up without complaint, and he has convinced two of his neighbors to join him. This kind of civic responsibility is exactly what our community needs, and schools are uniquely positioned to instill it.

Third, requiring service ensures that all students benefit from these experiences, not just those who already have the initiative or family encouragement to volunteer. Some students might discover a passion for teaching, environmental work, or working with elderly populations that they never would have found otherwise. Without a requirement, these students might never have the chance to explore such interests.

To address the time concern, I suggest the requirement be reasonable, perhaps ten to fifteen hours per semester and flexible enough that students can choose activities aligned with their interests and schedules. Students could select from tutoring, environmental cleanup, food bank assistance, or other approved organizations, allowing them to find something meaningful rather than something imposed.

Community service should not be seen as punishment or a mere box to check. Instead, it can be an opportunity for personal growth and community impact. I believe that with proper flexibility and reasonable time requirements, this policy would benefit both students and our broader community significantly.

Thank you for considering my perspective on this important decision.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student

I am writing to share my thoughts on the question of whether all students should be required to perform community service. After considering the arguments on both sides, I believe that community service should be required, though with reasonable flexibility built into the program.

I understand why some students resist the idea. Between homework, extracurricular activities, part-time jobs, and family responsibilities, many students already feel stretched thin. Adding another obligation can seem overwhelming, and forcing someone to volunteer might seem to contradict the very spirit of volunteering, which is supposed to come from the heart. These are valid concerns that any policy should address.

However, I believe the benefits of a service requirement far outweigh these drawbacks. First, community service teaches skills and values that classroom learning cannot. When my friend Maria began tutoring elementary students in reading, she didn't just help those children improve their skills. She also learned patience, communication, and leadership by figuring out how to explain concepts in different ways. These are qualities that will serve her well in college and in her future career, regardless of what path she chooses.

Second, requiring service ensures that every student experiences its benefits, not just those who already have volunteering instilled by their families. My friend Jake never considered community service until our school required him to log ten hours. He chose to help clean up litter in the park near school, and midway through the project, he told me he felt genuinely proud of what he had accomplished. Without the requirement, he might never have discovered this sense of purpose. A requirement can introduce students to something they would never have tried, and give them the chance to find, as Jake did, that they actually enjoy it.

Third, service requirements benefit our community as a whole. Schools have hundreds of students, and if even a fraction of them dedicate a few hours to worthwhile causes, the impact multiplies quickly. Litter gets removed from parks, younger children get academic support, and elderly neighbors receive company and assistance. This is a tangible good that our school could bring to the surrounding neighborhood.

To address concerns about time, I suggest keeping the requirement modest, perhaps ten to fifteen hours per year, and allowing students to choose from a wide range of approved activities so they can find something meaningful to them rather than something that feels forced.

Community service teaches valuable lessons, exposes students to new experiences, and strengthens our community. I hope you will consider implementing this requirement.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student

Distance learning has evolved from a niche accommodation into a mainstream educational option, and this shift benefits students in meaningful ways. While traditional classrooms will always have their place, the ability to attend classes from home offers flexibility, accessibility, and personalized learning that many students genuinely need.

First, distance learning removes barriers that prevent capable students from succeeding. Students who commute long distances, those with chronic illnesses, or those juggling family responsibilities often struggle to maintain consistent attendance in physical classrooms. A student caring for a younger sibling after a parent's work schedule changes, for instance, might miss crucial lessons entirely without the option to join remotely. Online access ensures that education continues even when circumstances make physical presence difficult or impossible.

Second, remote learning allows students to work at a pace suited to their individual needs. In a traditional classroom, a teacher must move at a speed that serves the majority, inevitably leaving some students behind while others grow bored. When learning happens through recorded lectures or flexible video sessions, students can pause, rewind, and revisit difficult concepts until they truly understand them. A student struggling with a complex math problem can replay the explanation multiple times without feeling embarrassed or holding up the rest of the class, while a student who grasps the material quickly can move ahead rather than waiting.

Third, distance learning teaches valuable skills that extend beyond academic content. Managing one's own schedule, staying organized without constant supervision, and communicating through digital platforms are increasingly essential in a world where remote work and virtual collaboration are common. Students who learn to navigate online coursework develop self-discipline and technological fluency that will serve them well in college and future careers, where many will encounter hybrid or fully remote work environments.

Critics argue that distance learning isolates students and weakens the social development that comes from in-person interaction. This concern has merit, particularly for younger children who benefit enormously from face-to-face relationships and hands-on collaboration. However, this does not mean distance learning must replace traditional schooling entirely. Rather, offering it as an option allows students and families to choose what works best for their circumstances. A student managing anxiety, for example, might thrive with the reduced social pressure of a remote classroom, while still participating in extracurricular activities that foster social connection.

Ultimately, distance learning should not be viewed as a replacement for traditional education but as a valuable option within it. By offering students the choice to attend classes from home, schools acknowledge that learning is not one-size-fits-all. Flexibility, accessibility, and skill-building make distance learning a worthwhile addition to modern education, empowering students to succeed on their own terms.

As a constituent who cares deeply about fair representation, I believe every American's vote should carry equal weight, regardless of which state they call home.

This creates an unequal system where the principle of "one person, one vote" is not truly honored. Furthermore, the winner-take-all method used by most states means that if a candidate wins a state by even a single vote, they receive all of that state's electoral votes. This discourages voter turnout in states that reliably favor one party, since residents may feel their vote does not matter. Another counterargument is that the Electoral College has provided stability throughout our nation's history, and changing it could lead to unforeseen complications. Sincerely,
A Concerned Constituent

The development of driverless cars represents one of the most significant technological advancements of our generation, and despite the concerns that accompany any major innovation, the benefits of autonomous vehicles far outweigh the risks. As this technology continues to evolve, society should embrace driverless cars as a means of improving safety, increasing accessibility, and transforming daily life for the better.

One of the strongest arguments in favor of driverless cars is their potential to drastically reduce traffic accidents. Human error—whether from distracted driving, fatigue, or impaired judgment—causes the vast majority of car accidents on the road today. Driverless cars, equipped with sensors, cameras, and sophisticated computer systems, do not suffer from these human limitations. They can react faster than a human driver, maintain constant awareness of their surroundings, and follow traffic laws without exception. By removing the unpredictable nature of human behavior from the equation, autonomous vehicles have the potential to save thousands of lives each year.

In addition to improving safety, driverless cars offer greater independence and mobility to individuals who currently struggle with transportation. Elderly citizens who can no longer safely operate a vehicle, people with disabilities that prevent them from driving, and others who lack access to reliable transportation would all benefit from a world where cars can drive themselves. This technology has the power to grant freedom and independence to populations who have long been limited by their inability to drive, allowing them to travel to work, medical appointments, and social engagements without relying on others.

Critics of driverless cars often point to concerns such as technological malfunctions, job losses in the transportation industry, and the high cost of development. While these concerns are valid and deserve attention, they should not overshadow the long-term benefits of this technology. Just as any new invention requires time to be perfected, driverless cars will improve as engineers refine the software and address safety concerns. Additionally, while some jobs may be affected, new industries and job opportunities will likely emerge as this technology develops, from vehicle maintenance to software engineering.

In conclusion, the development of driverless cars should be strongly supported, as the benefits of increased safety, accessibility, and convenience outweigh the challenges associated with this emerging technology. Though concerns about cost and job displacement are legitimate, they represent obstacles to be solved rather than reasons to abandon progress altogether. As with any transformative technology, driverless cars will require time and refinement, but their potential to save lives and improve mobility makes them a worthwhile investment in our future.

Using details from the article, write an essay arguing whether the use of this technology to read the emotional expressions of students in a classroom is valuable.
full_text:
The Facial Action Coding System, which allows computers to detect and interpret human emotions through subtle facial movements, represents a fascinating leap in technology. This system works by breaking down facial expressions into specific muscle movements, allowing a computer to recognize emotions like confusion, interest, boredom, or frustration with impressive accuracy. When applied to the classroom setting, this technology holds significant value, though it must be implemented thoughtfully to truly benefit students and teachers alike.

One of the most compelling arguments for using this technology in classrooms is its potential to help teachers respond to student needs in real time. Traditionally, a teacher must rely on visual cues, verbal feedback, or test scores to gauge whether students understand a lesson. However, these methods are often delayed or incomplete—a student might not raise their hand to admit confusion, or a quiz might only reveal a misunderstanding after the material has already been covered. The Facial Action Coding System offers a way to detect confusion or disengagement the moment it happens, giving educators the opportunity to adjust their teaching immediately. This could mean rephrasing a difficult concept, slowing down, or offering additional examples before students fall further behind.

Furthermore, this technology could serve as a valuable tool for identifying patterns over time. If a computer system consistently detects boredom or frustration during certain types of lessons, teachers could use this data to redesign their curriculum or teaching methods to be more engaging. This kind of large-scale, consistent feedback would be difficult for a human teacher to gather alone, especially in a classroom with many students. The ability to aggregate emotional data could lead to more personalized and effective education, as teachers could tailor their approach to the specific emotional and cognitive needs of their students.

However, there are legitimate concerns about privacy and the ethical implications of constantly monitoring students' facial expressions. Students may feel uncomfortable knowing their emotions are being tracked, and there is a risk that this technology could be misused to unfairly judge or label students based on incomplete data. Emotional expressions can be complex and context-dependent, and a computer might misinterpret a student's genuine reaction.

Despite these concerns, the benefits of using the Facial Action Coding System in classrooms outweigh the risks, provided it is used responsibly and transparently. When implemented with proper safeguards, this technology can enhance the learning experience by providing teachers with real-time insights that were previously unattainable. Ultimately, this innovation has the potential to revolutionize education by making classrooms more responsive to the emotional and cognitive needs of every student.

full_text:
Dear Principal Martinez,

I am writing to share my thoughts on the proposed policy that would require students to maintain a B average in order to participate in sports and other extracurricular activities. While I understand the intention behind this policy is to encourage academic achievement, I believe it would ultimately do more harm than good, and I urge you to reconsider this change.

First, extracurricular activities are often the very reason students stay motivated to come to school and work hard in their classes. Many students who maintain a C average are not lazy or unmotivated; they simply struggle with certain subjects or learn differently than others. For these students, sports, clubs, or band might be the one part of their day that gives them a sense of purpose and belonging. If we take that away because of a grade requirement, we risk losing their engagement with school altogether. A student who feels disconnected from school activities is far more likely to disengage academically as well, creating a downward spiral rather than an improvement.

Second, extracurricular activities themselves often teach skills that translate directly into academic success. Time management, teamwork, discipline, and perseverance are all lessons learned on the field, in the theater, or in a club meeting. Removing these activities from a struggling student's life does not give them more time to succeed—it removes one of the few structured, positive influences in their schedule. Without practice or rehearsal to attend, some students may simply fill that time with less productive, or even harmful, activities.

Additionally, this policy would disproportionately affect students who already face challenges outside of school, such as family responsibilities, financial struggles, or learning difficulties. These students may need extra support to raise their grades, not additional obstacles. Punishing them by removing extracurricular activities—often their only positive outlet—seems unfair and counterproductive.

Instead of an outright ban, I would suggest a more supportive approach. For example, students with a C average could be required to attend mandatory tutoring or study hall sessions in addition to their practices or rehearsals. This would encourage academic improvement while still allowing students to remain connected to their activities and communities. Coaches and activity sponsors could also be asked to monitor grades and provide encouragement or accountability.

I believe that school should be a place where every student can find both academic and personal growth. Please consider maintaining a policy that supports struggling students rather than isolating them further. Thank you for taking the time to consider student perspectives on this important issue.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student

Dear Principal Reyes,

I am writing to share my views on the proposed policy that would require students to maintain at least a B average in order to participate in sports or other extracurricular activities. While I understand the intention behind this policy is to encourage academic achievement, I believe it would do more harm than good, and I respectfully urge you to reconsider it.

First, extracurricular activities often serve as motivation for students to stay in school and work harder in their classes. Many students with C averages join sports teams or clubs because these activities give them a reason to show up, stay engaged, and feel connected to their school community. If we take these activities away from students who are struggling academically, we remove one of the very things that keeps them invested in school. Instead of improving their grades, this policy could cause some students to disengage entirely, leading to higher dropout rates and more discipline problems.

Second, sports and clubs teach valuable life skills that cannot be learned in a classroom alone. Teamwork, time management, leadership, and perseverance are all skills developed through participation in extracurricular activities. A student who struggles with math tests might excel as a team captain on the soccer field, learning responsibility and confidence that will help them in every area of life, including their studies. Denying these opportunities to students with lower grades punishes them for their academic struggles rather than helping them grow as well-rounded individuals.

Third, this policy could disproportionately affect students who already face challenges outside of school, such as family responsibilities, part-time jobs, or learning differences. These students may need extra support, not additional barriers. Instead of banning them from activities, the school could offer tutoring programs, study halls, or mentoring specifically for student-athletes and club members who need academic help. This would address the root problem—academic struggles—without punishing students by taking away activities that often provide stability and motivation in their lives.

Finally, research consistently shows that students involved in extracurricular activities tend to have better attendance and lower dropout rates, even if their grades are not perfect. Removing these activities could inadvertently lower overall academic performance by removing the very structure that keeps some students on track.

I ask that you consider alternative solutions, such as mandatory study sessions or grade check-ins with coaches and advisors, rather than an outright ban. This would support academic growth while allowing students to remain engaged in the activities that keep them connected to our school community.

Thank you for considering the student perspective on this important issue.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student

# A Letter to Principal Regarding the Proposed Grade Requirement Policy

Dear Principal Martinez,

I am writing to share my perspective on the proposed policy requiring a B average for participation in sports and extracurricular activities. While I understand the intention behind this policy is to encourage academic excellence, I believe implementing such a strict requirement would ultimately harm many students and should not be adopted.

First, extracurricular activities often serve as motivation for students to stay in school and maintain their grades in the first place. Many students with C averages participate in sports specifically because it gives them a reason to attend school regularly and stay engaged. If we remove this incentive by making the requirement too difficult to meet, we risk losing these students' interest in school altogether. Rather than pushing them to improve, we may push them away from education entirely.

Second, sports and clubs teach valuable life skills that classroom instruction alone cannot provide. Through athletics, students learn teamwork, discipline, time management, and perseverance. A student who struggles with academic subjects might excel on the basketball court or in the debate club, discovering confidence and leadership abilities that eventually translate into improved classroom performance. Denying these students access to activities where they can succeed may lower their self-esteem and motivation across the board.

Third, this policy would disproportionately affect students who already face academic challenges, whether due to learning differences, difficult home situations, or the need to work part-time jobs. These students often benefit most from the structure and support that team environments provide, including mentorship from coaches and the camaraderie of teammates who encourage them to keep trying. Removing this support system could cause struggling students to fall even further behind.

Instead of an outright ban, I propose a more balanced approach: requiring students with C averages to maintain a minimum GPA of 2.0 and attend mandatory tutoring sessions or study halls in exchange for continued participation. This would hold students accountable while still allowing them the benefits of extracurricular involvement. Coaches and activity sponsors could also implement grade checks throughout the season, requiring improvement rather than perfection.

I understand your goal is to prioritize academics, and I share that goal. However, I believe extracurricular activities are not obstacles to academic success but rather tools that can help achieve it. I respectfully ask that you consider a more flexible policy that supports struggling students rather than excluding them.

Thank you for considering my perspective and for seeking student input on this important decision.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student

# The Case Against Mandatory Extracurricular Activities

Requiring every student to participate in at least one extracurricular activity might seem like a well-intentioned way to build a more engaged school community, but this policy is ultimately misguided. While extracurricular activities offer genuine benefits, forcing participation undermines the very purpose these activities are meant to serve.

First, extracurricular activities are valuable precisely because they are voluntary. When students choose to join the debate team or try out for soccer, they bring enthusiasm and commitment that makes the experience meaningful. A student forced into an activity they have no interest in will likely become a reluctant participant who drags down the group's energy rather than contributing to it. Imagine a yearbook committee filled with half-hearted, mandatory members who resent being there—the quality of the publication would suffer, and so would the experience for students who genuinely wanted to be involved.

Second, this policy fails to account for the diverse circumstances of students' lives. Many students already carry heavy responsibilities outside of school. Some work part-time jobs to help support their families financially. Others serve as caregivers for younger siblings or grandparents while their parents work multiple jobs. Still others dedicate significant time to activities the school doesn't recognize, such as religious education, community volunteering, or intensive academic tutoring. For these students, adding a mandatory school activity isn't an enriching addition to their lives—it's an unwelcome burden that increases stress and takes time away from responsibilities that matter more to their families.

Third, mandatory participation can actually diminish the value of extracurricular involvement for everyone. Colleges and employers value extracurricular participation partly because it demonstrates genuine initiative and passion. If participation becomes universal and compulsory, it loses this distinguishing quality. A club advisor writing a recommendation letter for a truly dedicated student will find it harder to convey that dedication if every student technically "participated" in some activity, regardless of effort or interest.

Finally, this policy assumes that personal growth only happens through formally recognized school activities. Yet many students develop discipline, teamwork, and leadership skills through experiences the school doesn't track—learning an instrument independently, training for a marathon, or managing a small business selling crafts online. Forcing these students into unrelated extracurriculars ignores the meaningful development already happening in their lives.

Rather than mandating participation, schools should focus on making extracurricular activities more accessible and appealing through better funding, flexible scheduling, and diverse offerings. Genuine encouragement, not compulsion, will foster the kind of engaged, enthusiastic participation that benefits both students and their school community.

Cell phones have become extensions of ourselves, buzzing with notifications that feel impossible to ignore. Yet when a driver reaches for that phone behind the wheel, a routine drive can turn deadly in seconds. Drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle, because the risks to human life far outweigh the convenience of staying constantly connected.

The primary argument against cell phone use while driving rests on simple physics and human cognition. A vehicle traveling at fifty-five miles per hour covers over eighty feet per second. In the time it takes to glance at a text message, a driver can travel the length of a football field without truly watching the road. Studies from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration consistently show that distracted driving contributes to thousands of fatalities annually in the United States alone. This is not a matter of personal preference or convenience; it is a matter of public safety that affects everyone sharing the road, including pedestrians, cyclists, and passengers who have no say in a driver's decision to check their phone.

Some argue that hands-free technology solves this problem, allowing drivers to talk without physically holding a device. However, research reveals that the danger lies not in the hands but in the mind. Cognitive distraction occurs whether a driver holds a phone or uses voice commands, because the brain cannot fully focus on both a conversation and the complex task of driving simultaneously. This phenomenon, known as inattentional blindness, means drivers can look directly at a hazard—a pedestrian stepping into a crosswalk, a car braking suddenly—and fail to truly register it because their attention is divided. Banning only handheld use, then, addresses merely the visible symptom rather than the underlying disease.

Critics might also claim that a complete ban infringes on personal freedom or that emergencies require phone access. Yet freedom does not extend to actions that endanger others, just as one's freedom to swing a fist ends at another person's face. For genuine emergencies, pulling over takes only moments and costs little compared to the potential loss of life. Additionally, most emergencies can wait the few minutes until a driver reaches a safe stopping point.

Ultimately, the convenience of instant communication cannot justify the preventable deaths and injuries caused by distracted driving. Legislators and drivers alike must recognize that no text, call, or notification is worth a human life. By eliminating cell phone use entirely while driving, society can protect not only individual drivers but every person who shares the road with them. The choice between a phone call and a life should never be a difficult one.

Prompt: Some schools require students to complete summer projects to assure they continue learning during their break. Should these summer projects be teacher-designed or student-designed? Take a position on this question. Support your response with reasons and specific examples.
full_text:
Summer projects exist to keep young minds active during months when structured learning falls away. The question of who should design these projects—teachers or students—matters because the answer shapes whether students see summer work as meaningful growth or empty obligation. Student-designed projects, with teacher guidance and clear standards, offer the better path forward because they foster genuine engagement, develop critical life skills, and produce deeper, more lasting learning.

When students choose their own projects, they invest in the outcome. A teacher-assigned worksheet packet or a mandatory book report on a book nobody selected often becomes a chore to be finished rather than knowledge to be gained. Consider two students facing a summer science requirement. One is handed a packet of standardized problems to complete by August. The other decides to build a small hydroponic garden after become curious about sustainable farming. The second student will likely spend more time, ask better questions, and retain more knowledge, simply because the project sprang from authentic curiosity rather than obligation. Motivation is not a minor detail in learning; it is often the deciding factor between memorization and true understanding.

Student-designed projects also teach skills that fixed assignments cannot. Planning a project from scratch requires students to set goals, budget time, anticipate obstacles, and adjust when things go wrong—skills that mirror real-world problem-solving far more closely than following a teacher's checklist. A student who decides to teach herself basic guitar over the summer must figure out how to structure practice time, find resources, and measure her own progress. This kind of self-directed learning builds independence and resilience, qualities that serve students well beyond any single assignment.

Critics argue that without teacher oversight, students might choose projects that are too easy or lack academic rigor. This concern is valid but does not require eliminating student choice—it requires structured choice. Schools can require students to submit project proposals for teacher approval, ensuring the work meets certain learning objectives while still allowing students to select topics and methods that interest them. A student wanting to explore local history, for instance, might propose interviewing elderly community members and creating a short documentary. A teacher can review this proposal, suggest research components, and ensure it meets academic standards, all while preserving the student's ownership.

Ultimately, the goal of summer projects should be lasting engagement with learning, not the mere completion of a task. Projects designed by students, framed within teacher-approved goals, better achieve this goal. They cultivate curiosity, independence, and self-motivation, ensuring that summer becomes a season of genuine growth rather than another chapter of compulsory schoolwork.

Summer learning projects serve an important purpose: they prevent the academic slide that often occurs during long breaks and keep students intellectually engaged. However, the value of these projects depends heavily on who designs them. While teacher-designed projects offer structure and ensure curriculum alignment, student-designed projects are ultimately more effective because they foster genuine engagement, develop independent thinking skills, and better prepare students for the self-directed learning they will need throughout their lives.

The strongest argument for student-designed projects is motivation. When students choose topics that genuinely interest them, they invest more time and effort than when completing an assignment handed to them. Consider a student passionate about marine biology who designs a summer project studying a local watershed, tracking water quality, and researching the aquatic species living there. This student will likely spend hours beyond what is required, driven by curiosity rather than obligation. Contrast this with a generic teacher-assigned reading log that many students complete hastily the week before school resumes, extracting little genuine learning from the experience. When a student must decide what to study, how to structure their time, and how to demonstrate what they have learned, they practice metacognitive skills essential for success in college and careers. A student who designs a project building a small robotics kit must research materials, troubleshoot problems, and evaluate their own progress without a teacher's constant guidance. These are precisely the skills that standardized curricula often fail to develop, yet they are the skills employers and universities consistently say students lack.

Critics argue that student-designed projects risk being unfocused or academically weak, since students may lack the expertise to create rigorous learning experiences. Schools can require students to submit project proposals for teacher approval, meet certain learning objectives, or choose from a set of academic domains—math, science, literature, history—while still selecting their specific topic and approach within that domain. This hybrid model preserves accountability while granting meaningful choice.

Ultimately, the goal of summer learning should not simply be to prevent forgetting, but to cultivate lifelong learners who see education as something they actively pursue rather than passively receive.
